doc.title: Scott Jimmy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: From the funeral to a Warner Bros. contract
summary: Attention from the funeral led to a Warner contract and producer Tommy LiPuma.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: When was the first time that you heard, as a result of your performance at the funeral, there was interest in you as a recording artist again?

I’ll ask it again. When was the first time, after the funeral, you heard that there was interest in you as a recording artist – that people were beginning to talk about recording you, because they had heard you do Somebody to Watch over Me at the funeral? When did that happen? Who called you?
It was a little reporter that lived in Brooklyn. He called and told me what was going on.
Then did you hear from Seymour Stein? Did he call you? Or you don’t recall that?
Because what I’m trying to figure out is how – what led to making the album All the Way with Tommy LiPuma?

Actually, the attention came from the funeral. The attention came from the funeral, and they got together and got him. I think he did a good job for the recording, helping to produce the recording. I think Tommy did a good job.

Did you think – was all this taking you by surprise? Because it had been so long since you had had a record deal. To get a recording contract from Warner Bros. Records, which is a huge label, as a result of singing at the funeral and having Seymour Stein – who was a big-shot music mogul – hear you and able to give you a contract, and then give you one of the leading jazz producers in the country, must have been a big thrill? Or were you excited?
